1.title: Governing Release, Monitoring and Maintenance
1.text: Welcome to Module ten: Governing Release, Monitoring and Maintenance. This is the biggest competency of domain three. It follows the A I system from the moment it goes live: how to release it responsibly, how to keep watching it, how to test it harder from time to time, how to handle incidents, and what to disclose.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Assess readiness and prepare the release, including the model card and conformity. Monitor continuously and keep a schedule for maintenance, updates and retraining. Run periodic assessments: security tests, audits, red teaming and threat modeling. Handle and record incidents, issues and risks. Work with stakeholders to find why incidents happen. And make the disclosures that transparency duties require.

1.title: Case Check-In: Release, a Wrong Refund and a Shift in Applicants
1.text: At Helios, the hiring tool is ready for a gate review, and Daniel Osei brings the model card and the conformity evidence. Weeks after launch, the assistant tells a customer about a refund window that does not exist; the cause is out-of-date support documents. After a hiring campaign in a new region, monitoring flags a shift in the input data. Mei Tanaka's team plans a red-team test, and Lucia Moreno asks what Helios must disclose to candidates.

1.title: Release Readiness: The Gate and the Checklist
1.text: A release gate decides whether the system is ready for production. Tests are passed against the thresholds set earlier, and residual risks are accepted by the owner. Documentation is complete: the model card, the instructions for use and the technical documentation. Conformity requirements are satisfied where a law requires them. Operations are ready: a monitoring plan, a rollback or shutdown plan, support and training, and a communication plan. Missing items are conditions, not afterthoughts. Exam tip: readiness is wider than test results.

1.title: The Release Package: Model Card, Instructions and Records
1.text: The release package has several parts. The model card, from module nine: intended use, performance by group, evaluation conditions and limitations. The instructions for use for deployers: provider identity, capabilities and limits, oversight measures, resources and lifetime, and log collection, under Article thirteen. Technical documentation under Article eleven and Annex four, and the risk assessment record. Test reports, approvals and version identifiers. And the monitoring plan and incident contacts. Exam tip: the deployer can only oversee what the provider tells it.

1.title: Satisfying Conformity Requirements
1.text: For E U high-risk systems, complete the conformity assessment under Article forty-three, declare conformity under Article forty-seven, affix the C E marking under Article forty-eight, and register under Article forty-nine, all before placing the system on the market. A substantial modification after release needs a new assessment, though changes pre-determined for a learning system are not substantial. Elsewhere, sector rules, state laws and contract commitments may add checks. Standards such as I S O forty-two thousand and one can help organize the evidence. Exam tip: conformity comes before market placement.

1.title: Staged Release and Rollback
1.text: Release in stages. Start with a small share of users, then widen as monitoring stays healthy. Use feature flags and canaries to turn parts on and off and to compare against the old version. Agree rollback criteria: the thresholds that trigger a return to the previous version or a pause. Have a kill switch, a tested way to stop the system; N I S T asks for mechanisms to supersede, disengage or deactivate. And make support ready. At Helios, the hiring tool starts in one region. Exam tip: an untested rollback is not a rollback plan.

1.title: What to Monitor
1.text: Monitor six families. Performance: accuracy and error rates against the thresholds. Data and drift: changes in inputs and outputs over time. Fairness: outcomes by group, compared with launch. Safety and security: abuse, attacks and harmful outputs. Usage and feedback: volume, complaints, appeals and human overrides. And operations: latency, availability and cost. N I S T Measure three point one asks for approaches to track existing, unanticipated and emergent risks. Exam tip: monitor what can go wrong for people, not only for the server.

1.title: Drift: Data, Concept and Model
1.text: Drift comes in three forms. Data drift: the mix of inputs changes, as when Helios gets applicants from a new region. Concept drift: the relationship between inputs and the right answer changes, as with a new refund policy. Performance drift: accuracy or fairness falls, and it may lag the other two. Detect drift by comparing input distributions and outputs with the training baseline, and tracking metrics by group. React by investigating, retraining or recalibrating, or rolling back, then retesting. Exam tip: data drift can appear before accuracy drops.

1.title: Maintenance, Updates and Retraining
1.text: A maintenance schedule sets regular reviews, security patches, dependency updates and data refreshes. Scheduled retraining keeps the model current, while triggered retraining responds to drift, incidents, new data or a new law. Every change goes through change control: test, approve, release in stages and monitor. A substantial modification may need a new conformity assessment, as module six said. Document each version: data, settings, results and approver. And retire the model when it cannot be kept safe or useful. Exam tip: retraining is a change like any other.

1.title: Monitoring in Practice: Owners, Thresholds, Alerts, Logs
1.text: Monitoring in practice needs five things. Owners: each metric has a named owner and a review rhythm. Thresholds and alerts: warning and action levels, with who is paged. Logs: the system records events for traceability, under Article twelve, and logs are kept for the period the rules require. Human review of samples: people read a sample of real outputs, because metrics miss some failures. Escalation: alerts above the action level go to the incident process. And the provider's post-market monitoring plan, under Article seventy-two. Exam tip: monitoring without owners and escalation is just data collection.

1.title: Periodic Assessment: What, How Often, Who
1.text: Continuous monitoring watches the live system. Periodic assessments step back and test it harder. Audits check compliance with policy and law. Red teaming tries to make the system fail or misbehave. Threat modeling maps how an attacker could reach and abuse the system. Security testing looks for vulnerabilities in code, models and infrastructure. Set frequency by risk, and also run them after major changes. Exam tip: policy compliance is an audit, breaking the system is red teaming, and mapping attack paths is threat modeling.

1.title: Audits of AI Systems
1.text: Audits take several forms. Internal audit is the third line, checking governance and risk management, as in module two. An external or independent audit examines compliance and controls, and I S O forty-two thousand and one certification relies on audits of the management system. The scope covers policy compliance, data and model records, testing evidence, monitoring and incident handling. Evidence is documents, logs, test results and interviews. Outputs are findings with owners and due dates. Some laws, such as New York City's rule for hiring tools, require independent bias audits. Exam tip: an audit looks backward at evidence.

1.title: Red Teaming
1.text: Red teaming is a structured attempt to make the system fail or misbehave, as a determined misuser would. Methods include misuse and jailbreak attempts, bias probes, data-extraction attempts and harmful-output tests. Independent testers see what builders miss, so mix internal and external skills. Findings are rated, fixed and retested. The A I Act requires adversarial testing for general-purpose models with systemic risk, in Article fifty-five. At Helios, Mei Tanaka's team tests the assistant for abuse and data leakage. Exam tip: red teaming is broader than normal acceptance testing.

1.title: Threat Modeling and AI-Specific Attacks
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Threat modeling lists assets, attackers, entry points and abuse cases, then plans controls. Know five A I-specific attacks by description. Data poisoning: tampering with training data. Evasion: inputs crafted to cause mistakes. Model extraction: copying a model by querying it. Inversion and membership inference: recovering or detecting training data. Prompt injection: hidden instructions in input that hijack a language model. Reference lists exist: MITRE ATLAS, the Adversarial Threat Landscape for A I Systems, and the O W A S P, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, Top Ten for L L M Applications. Exam tip: recognize each attack by its description.

1.title: Security Testing, Reliability and Safety Checks
1.text: Security testing includes penetration tests of the application and its interfaces, vulnerability scans, and tests for leakage and access control. Model-level tests add adversarial inputs, poisoning checks, extraction and inversion attempts, and prompt-injection tests. Reliability checks look at performance under stress, noise and drift, failover and recovery. Safety checks ask whether outputs or actions harm people in foreseeable use or misuse. Check third-party models, data and components too. Record results, fix findings, and feed them into the risk register. Exam tip: security, reliability and safety are three different questions.

1.title: What Counts as an AI Incident
1.text: An incident is an event in which an A I system causes or could cause harm, or fails or behaves unexpectedly. Examples: a wrong or harmful output, a biased outcome pattern, a data leak, a security breach, a safety event, or an outage that affects people. Near misses matter: log them and learn. An issue is a smaller problem to fix, and a risk is something that may happen, so keep separate registers, linked. Severity depends on harm to people, legal duties and scale. Exam tip: a near miss is cheap information.

1.title: The Incident Response Cycle
1.text: Incident response has six steps. Detect and report: monitoring, users, staff or a partner raises it. Triage: set severity and an owner. Contain: pause, limit or correct the system to stop further harm. Investigate: find the root cause. Remediate and retest, then communicate to those affected and to authorities where required. And learn: update tests, thresholds and documents. Document at every step. Exam tip: contain before you investigate. Stop the harm first, then find the cause.

1.title: Reporting Clocks and Records
1.text: Several clocks can start at once. Under the E U A I Act, Article seventy-three, a provider reports a serious incident not later than fifteen days after awareness, two days for a widespread infringement, and ten days after a death. Under the G D P R, Article thirty-three, a controller notifies a personal data breach not later than seventy-two hours after awareness, where feasible. Contracts may set shorter notice, and internal policy sets escalation. Communicate to affected people with plain information, as N I S T Manage four point three says. Exam tip: the shortest applicable limit governs.

1.title: Issue and Risk Registers, and Learning
1.text: Keep three linked registers. The risk register lists risks, likelihood and severity, controls, owners and status, and is updated after each incident. The issue log records problems found in operation, with severity, owner, due date and closure evidence. The incident register records every incident and near miss, with root cause and corrective actions. Repeated issues point to a systemic cause, so report trends to the committee. Record lessons learned. N I S T Manage four point one asks for appeal and override, decommissioning and recovery plans. Exam tip: an incident that changes nothing was not learned from.

2.title: Why AI Incidents Arise: Five Causes
2.text: Five causes explain many A I incidents. Brittleness: the system works only in narrow conditions and breaks outside them. Weak robustness: it fails under noise, odd inputs or attack. Poor data: stale, wrong or unrepresentative data, like the Helios refund error. Insufficient testing: a case or change that was never tested. And drift: the data or the world changed since training. Often several causes combine. Exam tip: name the cause from the symptom. Stale answers point to data, sudden failure on new inputs to brittleness, and slow decay to drift.

2.title: Root-Cause Analysis With Cross-Functional Teams
2.text: Why cross-functional? Because causes cross boundaries: data, model, process, content and use. Bring data science, engineering, the business owner, content owners, legal and privacy, security and support. Use methods such as a timeline of events, five whys, and a cause-and-effect diagram. Keep the review blameless: find system causes, not culprits. The output is causes, corrective actions, owners and dates. At Helios, support content owners join data science to trace the refund error. Exam tip: a purely technical review misses process and content causes.

2.title: Helios: Two Incidents, Two Root Causes
2.text: Helios had two incidents. The wrong refund window came from out-of-date support documents in the retrieval source: poor data and weak change control. The corrective actions are to refresh and version the documents, add an owner and a review date, and test answers against policy changes. The shift in input data after the new-region campaign is data drift: the applicant mix changed. The actions are to retest fairness and performance on the new mix, retrain or recalibrate, and add drift alerts. The common thread: the data changed and nobody owned the change. Exam tip: fix the process, not only the single wrong answer.

2.title: From Cause to Prevention
2.text: Match every cause to a control. Poor data: data owners, freshness rules, quality checks at the source and change control. Insufficient testing: regression tests for every incident, and test sets that include edge cases and policy changes. Brittleness and weak robustness: stress and adversarial testing, input validation, and fallbacks to a person. Drift: monitoring with alerts, and scheduled and triggered retraining. Governance: update the risk register, thresholds and instructions after each incident, and share lessons with deployers and authorities. Exam tip: every incident should add a test.

2.title: Public Disclosures: What, to Whom
2.text: Disclosures follow the audience. Authorities and assessors receive technical documentation and logs on request. Deployers receive instructions for use, capabilities and limits, and oversight measures, under Article thirteen. People affected and users receive notices that A I is used and, where required, explanations, as in Article fifty and modules four and six. The public receives registration entries and summaries where the law requires them. At Helios, candidates are told that A I screens applications, and how to ask for a person. Exam tip: documentation to authorities, instructions to deployers, notices to people.

2.title: Instructions for Use and Technical Documentation
2.text: Instructions for use must be clear and accessible to deployers. They state the provider's identity, the capabilities and limitations, pre-determined changes, human oversight measures, resources and lifetime, and log collection, under Article thirteen. Technical documentation, under Article eleven and Annex four, is kept current and supplied to authorities on request. Accuracy levels and metrics are declared in the instructions, under Article fifteen. Update both when the system changes. Deployers use the instructions to meet their own duties, so gaps pass downstream. Exam tip: vague instructions mean the deployer cannot oversee properly.

2.title: Post-Market Plans, Registration and Public Summaries
2.text: This slide is tagged verify live. The post-market monitoring plan is part of the technical documentation, under Article seventy-two, and shows how the provider will watch the system after release. Information registered for high-risk systems under Article forty-nine is publicly accessible in a user-friendly form, except one protected section, according to Article seventy-one. General-purpose model providers publish a training-content summary, as module six said. Hiring tools in New York City need a public summary of the independent bias audit. As of the twenty-seventh of October, twenty twenty-six, disclosure rules are still developing. Exam tip: public disclosure is limited and specific.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. Release: a gate on tests, documents, conformity, approvals, monitoring and rollback, with a staged rollout. Monitoring and maintenance: performance, data drift, fairness, safety, usage and operations, with owners and thresholds, and scheduled and triggered retraining under change control. Periodic assessment: security testing, audits, red teaming and threat modeling, and five A I attack types. Incidents: contain, investigate, remediate, communicate and learn, with clocks of fifteen, ten and two days and seventy-two hours. Causes: brittleness, weak robustness, poor data, thin testing and drift. And disclosures by audience.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Helios's hiring tool passes all its tests, but its model card is incomplete and no monitoring plan exists. What should the release gate decide? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Readiness covers tests, documentation, approvals, monitoring and rollback together. A system that cannot be monitored or explained is not ready.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Which two items belong in the release readiness review of a high-risk E U system? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. A release review checks conformity evidence and operational readiness, including a tested rollback and a monitoring plan with owners and thresholds. Event planning, commissions and visual design are not readiness criteria.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A deployed model's input data start to differ from its training data, but accuracy has not yet fallen. What is happening, and what should the team do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A change in the input mix is data drift, an early warning that can come before a fall in accuracy. Investigate, retrain or recalibrate if needed, and retest.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Which approach best fits a model whose data change quickly? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A schedule keeps the model current, triggers respond to drift and incidents, and change control tests and approves each new version. Never retraining, untested automatic deployment and waiting for complaints are all weak.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Which two activities are periodic assessments of an A I system's performance, reliability and safety? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Red teaming and independent audits are periodic assessments, alongside threat modeling and security testing. The other activities have nothing to do with assessing the system.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. The Helios assistant tells a customer about a refund window that does not exist. What is the best response sequence? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Contain the harm, log the incident, find the root cause, fix and retest, and communicate as required. Waiting, renaming or deleting evidence makes the problem worse.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. After a hiring campaign in a new region, the applicant mix changes and a model's results shift. Which cause of A I incidents does this best illustrate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A changed input mix is data drift: the model now sees data unlike its training data. Interface layout, passwords and hardware are not the cause.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. Who should take part in the root-cause review of the wrong refund answer? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The causes cross data, model, content, process and legal duties, so the review needs the people who own each link in the chain, not a single function.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. Which of these is made publicly available for a high-risk system under the E U A I Act? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Information registered in the E U database is publicly accessible in a user-friendly form, with one protected section. Technical documentation and logs go to authorities on request, and internal registers and test reports are not published.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all nine answers. Question one: B. Question two: C and E. Question three: D. Question four: A. Question five: B and D. Question six: C. Question seven: B. Question eight: D. Question nine: A. That completes Module ten, and with it domain three. Next, domain four begins with Module eleven: the decision to deploy.
